references.text: Expands on the prohibition against charging interest to poor Israelites and the command to help those in need among the people.
Concerns the duty to lend to poor brothers without being harsh toward them, especially in connection with the year of release.
Repeats the prohibition against taking interest from a brother but permits it from foreigners.
Nehemiah rebukes the people for charging interest from their brothers and demands that they stop this practice.
Describes the righteous as one who does not lend money at interest.
Warns that wealth accumulated through interest and usury will ultimately go to the one who is kind to the poor.
The righteous is described as one who takes no interest or usury.
God accuses Israel of taking interest and usury and exploiting their neighbor.
Jesus teaches about lending without expecting anything in return, showing mercy to all.
A direct legal parallel that extends the prohibition against interest to also include food trade.
Matthew expands on the principle by moving from 'do not take interest' to 'give without expectation of repayment'.
Ezekiel uses the prohibition against interest as a central criterion for righteousness and life.
Almost identical legal text confirming that the purpose is to ensure life and brotherhood.
Luke starts from the prohibition against interest and encourages even greater generosity without expectation.
